key_insight: AI agents operating in multi-agent "societies" can fail even when they are honest and capable, because current harnesses and messaging protocols do not adequately support coordination across trust boundaries. The paper shows that malicious or faulty agents can exploit these weaknesses to stall collaboration and steer outcomes.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of safely coordinating autonomous AI agents that represent different principals with only partially aligned goals. It highlights the need for a stronger "social harness" to manage communication, trust, and resilience against manipulation in agentic societies.
method: Experimentally evaluate existing harnesses and messaging primitives in multi-agent settings where agents must coordinate autonomously.
Test both honest competent agents and faulty or malicious agents to observe failure modes in collaboration and outcome quality.
Analyze how vulnerabilities in communication and coordination can be exploited to block progress or influence decisions.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work is a warning that agentic systems need more than task performance—they need robust social infrastructure for trust, coordination, and adversarial resistance. It is especially relevant for deploying multi-agent workflows in real-world settings with partially conflicting objectives.
visual_elements: A trust-boundary diagram showing multiple agents representing different principals.
A failure-flow illustration of how a malicious agent can stall or redirect collaboration.
A side-by-side comparison of existing harnesses versus a proposed social harness.
An icon-based summary of risks: trust, manipulation, deadlock, and miscoordination.
paper_title: Agentic Societies Need a Social Harness
paper_authors: Tapan Chugh, Vidushi Singh, Krish Jain, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Ratul Mahajan
